lines.text: New in the Netherlands: if you come to the Netherlands because your partner lives here, you usually go to live with your partner.
If you are a vluchteling, you usually first come to an asylum seekers' center [asielzoekerscentrum (AZC)].
If you have a residence permit [verblijfsvergunning] and no partner here, you usually first get a home through the municipality [gemeente]; you then do not have much choice.
Free rental sector [Vrije sector]: if you earn enough money, you can look for a home in the free rental sector.
The rent there is high, though.
You can look for houses through a private individual [particulier]: a real estate agent [makelaar] or a landlord [huisbaas].
A real estate agent helps people buy or sell a house, but sometimes also helps find a rental home.
You can also search through a housing corporation [woningcorporatie]: such an organization takes care of building, renting out [verhuren] and maintaining [onderhouden] homes.
Social housing [Sociale huur]: if you do not earn very much, you can get a social rental home [sociale huurwoning].
The rent is not that high; there is a maximum rent price [maximale huurprijs].
Your first home with a residence permit is usually a social rental home.
If you want to rent on your own, you must quickly register [inschrijven] as a home seeker [woningzoekende] with one or more housing corporations (you usually pay money when registering).
After that, it can take a long time before you get a home.
A large family gets a larger home; with a higher income you can also get a larger home.
If you need a home very quickly (for example just divorced [gescheiden] with young children), you can get an urgency declaration [urgentieverklaring] from the municipality — not many people get one.
How exactly this works differs per municipality.
Rights and obligations: when you rent a house, you get a rental contract [huurcontract].

It contains your obligations to the landlord/lessor [verhuurder] (how much rent and when you pay), but also the rights of the tenant [huurder]: which repairs [reparaties] and which maintenance [onderhoud] the landlord must do, and the rules for terminating [opzeggen] the rental.
The landlord may not simply terminate your rental.
Complaints: do you have a complaint about the landlord (poor maintenance, too much rent)?
Then you must first report [melden] it to the landlord yourself, in an email or letter.
If that does not help, you can contact the rent tribunal [huurcommissie].
Rent allowance [Huurtoeslag]: some people can get part of the rent back from the Tax Administration [Belastingdienst].
This is only possible if you do not earn too much.
The less you earn per month, the more you get back.
Buying a house: you must earn enough, because a house costs a lot of money.
Almost everyone has to borrow money from a bank: the mortgage [hypotheek].
How much mortgage you can get depends on your income [inkomen].
Every month you pay a fixed amount [bedrag] back to the bank.
Most people buy through a real estate agent.
You must make an offer/bid [bod] on the house.
If you have the highest bid, you can usually buy it.
Then you go to the notary [notaris] to sign [tekenen] the contract.
OZB and parking tax: sometimes you also pay tax [belasting] to the municipality.
If you have bought a house, you pay property tax [onroerendezaakbelasting (OZB)]: the more your house is worth [waard], the more OZB.
If you live in a neighborhood with paid parking, you also pay parking tax [parkeerbelasting].
How much you pay differs per municipality.
